stem: A 7-year-old boy presents after a splash burn to the anterior trunk and upper arm, with an estimated burn size of 11% body surface area and haemodynamic stability; how should this burn be classified?

options.text: A minor burn because he is stable
A severe burn because it affects at least 10% body surface area
A minor burn because only one side of the body is involved
An outpatient burn because most paediatric burns are small
A moderate burn because it is limited to the trunk and arm

explanation: A severe burn is classified by burn extent, and any burn affecting 10% or more of body surface area meets that threshold. An 11% burn is therefore severe regardless of haemodynamic stability.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because haemodynamic stability does not change the size-based definition of a severe burn.
optionExplanations.B: Correct because a burn affecting at least 10% body surface area meets the severe-burn threshold.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because laterality is not the criterion for severity; percentage body surface area is.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because the classification depends on burn extent, and 11% body surface area is severe.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because the relevant severity threshold here is body surface area affected, not anatomical location.
